summary_responses.response: Overloads caused by miscoordination or attacks can make microservices reject valuable requests, while indiscriminate retries can worsen congestion. Researchers propose DiffTry, which gives high-priority requests more retry attempts than low-priority ones, improving their chances of success while reducing retry amplification. The lightweight, stateless mechanism requires no overload detection or coordination between services and can be deployed without changing application code. In an illustrative overload scenario, high-priority requests accounted for about 85% of successful completions despite representing half the incoming traffic. Analytical models, simulations, and a live Kubernetes deployment supported the approach, with measured rejection rates closely matching predictions.

key_fact_breakdown.key_fact: DiffTry (Differential Retries) is a stateless mechanism that assigns different retry-attempt limits to different priority classes of requests to achieve differentiation in rejection rates.
Under overload with DiffTry, high-priority requests achieve a rejection rate of around 15% and account for about 85% of successful completions when both classes contribute 50% of input load.
DiffTry requires neither overload sensing nor microservices coordination and is implemented as a drop-in service-mesh plugin requiring no application code changes.

The paper develops an analytical model for DiffTry starting with two services in tandem, then generalizes it to networks of services using an open-network model combined with flow classes and priorities.

The paper proves that network-wide class-level success rates increase monotonically with retry limits and validates the analysis on a live Kubernetes deployment where measured rejection closely matches the theoretical predictions.
DiffTry assigns different retry attempt limits to requests from different priority classes to prioritize high-value transactions during overload.

summary_responses.response: The FAA has issued an airworthiness directive for certain Bombardier BD-700-2A12 airplanes, effective November 18, 2026. summary_responses.response: The Office of Personnel Management issued a direct final rule updating federal Family and Medical Leave Act (FMLA) regulations to reflect statutory changes enacted in 2021 and 2023. Virtually all federal civilian service, including prior temporary or intermittent work, and certain honorable active military service count toward the 12-month requirement for FMLA and paid parental leave, although current temporary and intermittent employees remain ineligible for title 5 FMLA. The changes also clarify that employees may substitute annual or sick leave earned under non-title 5 authorities for unpaid FMLA leave. Veterans Health Administration employees covered by a separate VA leave system are excluded from title 5 FMLA coverage but retain family and medical leave rights under another law. The rule is set to take effect on December 14, 2026, unless significant adverse comments are received by November 16, in which case OPM will withdraw the affected provisions and issue a proposed rule.
